title: Fables and legends
def: Muslim scholars separate the Quran’s own stories from the later tales, many from Jewish and Christian lore, that entered commentaries (isrāʾīliyyāt).
what: The commentaries of the first centuries often add detail to the Quran’s stories from what was told by Jews and Christians who became Muslims. The Prophet is reported to have said: “Narrate from the Children of Israel; there is no harm” (Sahih al-Bukhari), and also “do not believe the People of the Book and do not disbelieve them” (Sahih al-Bukhari).
misread: That Islam teaches every fable that appears in Muslim books.
sources: Ibn Kathir and Ibn Taymiyya set the rule: accept only what agrees with the Quran and sound hadith, reject what contradicts them, and suspend judgement on the rest. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari of a monkey stoned for adultery is a saying of a follower, Amr ibn Maymun, and not of the Prophet, and many scholars have criticised it. The Quran’s own accounts are brief and give no such details.

title: Fahisha
def: Shameful and indecent conduct, and especially unlawful sexual relations, which the Quran forbids.
what: God forbids “shameful deeds, whether open or hidden” (7:33), and prayer “prevents shameful and wrong deeds” (29:45). For adultery the Quran requires proof by four eyewitnesses (4:15, 24:4) and punishes the one who accuses without proof with eighty lashes (24:4). Repentance and amendment are accepted (24:5, 4:16).
sources: The verses on punishment in 4:15–16 and 24:2 are read by jurists as stages of the law, and the very high standard of proof means that in practice conviction on witnesses alone is rare. The Prophet told people to conceal what they could, and to avoid suspicion.

title: Fal and istikhara
def: Islam forbids divination, but teaches the prayer of istikhara to ask God’s guidance in a decision.
what: The prayer of istikhara was taught by the Prophet: two units of prayer followed by a supplication, “O God, if You know that this matter is good for me in my religion and my life and the end of my affair, then decree it for me…” (Sahih al-Bukhari). It is a request for guidance, and not a way of foretelling the future.
sources: Opening the Quran at random to predict the outcome of a venture, a custom of some, is disliked by most scholars as an innovation, and the Prophet said that whoever goes to a diviner and believes him has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad (Abu Dawud).

title: Family
def: The Quran stresses ties of kinship, obedience to parents and mercy to children, and speaks of families reunited in Paradise (13:23).
what: “Fear God, in whose name you ask one another, and the wombs (kinship ties)” (4:1). The Quran says that the righteous will enter gardens of Eden “with whoever was righteous among their parents, spouses and offspring” (13:23, 40:8). The Prophet said that the one who cuts the ties of kinship will not enter Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim).

title: Faqir
def: A poor person; the Quran uses it for those in need (9:60), and the term is also used of Sufi ascetics.
what: The Quran lists the poor (fuqarāʾ) first among those who may receive zakat (9:60), and says that “you are the ones in need of God, and God is the Rich” (35:15). In Sufi usage faqīr means one who owns nothing before God.

title: Fatiha
def: The opening chapter of the Quran, recited in every unit of the prayer.
what: Its seven verses begin “In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds” and end with the prayer “guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have favoured, not of those who earn Your anger, nor of those who go astray” (1:1–7). The Prophet said that there is no prayer for one who does not recite it (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: Many commentators identified “those who earn anger” and “those who go astray” with Jews and Christians, from a hadith reported in al-Tirmidhi. Others, including many modern scholars, take the phrases as describing anyone who knows the truth and rejects it, or who strays from it without knowing, whatever his community.

title: Fatima
def: The Prophet’s youngest daughter, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.
what: Fatima (d. 632) was the only one of the Prophet’s children to survive him, dying about six months after him. The Prophet said that she is “part of me” (Sahih al-Bukhari) and “the leader of the women of Paradise” (al-Tirmidhi).

title: Fatra
def: A pause in revelation after the first revelations; some reports of the Prophet’s distress at that time are not from Aisha.
what: Revelation paused for a period after the first revelation at Hira, then resumed with chapter 74. The long report in Sahih al-Bukhari from Aisha ends with a sentence added by the narrator al-Zuhri, who says it reached him that the Prophet in his grief would go to the mountain tops to throw himself off.
misread: That Muhammad tried to kill himself.
sources: Hadith scholars such as Ibn Hajar point out that this sentence is al-Zuhri’s, “it has reached us”, and not part of Aisha’s account, so that it has no chain to the Prophet. The sound part of the report describes his fear and the comfort of Khadija, who said: “God will never disgrace you, for you keep family ties, bear the burdens of the weak and help in calamity.”

title: Fatwa
def: A legal opinion given by a qualified scholar (muftī) in answer to a question; it is not binding.
what: A fatwa states what a scholar judges the sources to require in a case. A questioner may take it to another scholar, and a ruling by one scholar can be opposed by another. In many countries an official mufti issues them, and in all of them the ruling is only as strong as its reasoning.
sources: Many Muslim scholars and authorities rejected it, saying that a sentence cannot be passed without a trial and a hearing, and that Islamic law does not allow Muslims to kill abroad on a decree from a ruler.

title: Fidya
def: A compensation, such as feeding the poor, in place of a fast or for a failure in the pilgrimage.
what: The Quran says that those who cannot fast owe “a ransom: the feeding of a poor person” (2:184), and sets compensation for certain violations of the state of pilgrimage: fasting, almsgiving or a sacrifice (2:196). Compensation of this kind is also required for broken oaths (5:89).

title: Fig and olive
def: Chapter 95, “The Fig”, swears by the fig and the olive, and by Mount Sinai and the safe city of Mecca.
what: “By the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinai, and this secure city” (95:1–3). The oaths are by places of prophets: the fig and olive lands of Syria-Palestine, where Jesus lived, Sinai, where Moses spoke with God, and Mecca. The chapter goes on to say that humanity was created in “the best form” (95:4).

title: Fighting
def: The Quran’s rules on fighting are limited: against those who attack, in defence, with justice, and ending when they stop.
what: Permission to fight was given after years of persecution, to those who are fought, because they were wronged (22:39), and it is limited: “fight in the way of God those who fight you, and do not transgress” (2:190). If the enemy inclines to peace, make peace (8:61). “If they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, God has given you no way against them” (4:90). The “sword verse” (9:5) is about those who broke a treaty, and it is followed by 9:6, which says that if a polytheist asks for protection, he must be given it.
misread: That the hadith “I was ordered to fight the people until they say there is no god but God” orders the killing of all non-Muslims.
sources: Scholars such as al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar explain that “the people” in the report are the idolaters of Arabia, who had attacked the Muslims, and not Jews, Christians or people at peace; the Prophet made treaties with them and took the jizya from the People of the Book. Verses on fighting are tied to their occasions, as asbab al-nuzul explains. The Prophet forbade killing women, children and monks.

title: Fingerprints
def: Verse 75:4 says God can restore the very fingertips of a person on the Day of Judgement.
what: “Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to restore in perfect order even his fingertips (banān)” (75:3–4). The translations say “fingertips”. Some modern Muslim writers have read it as a reference to fingerprints, which were not used in identification until the nineteenth century.
sources: The verse’s point is that God’s power reaches the finest detail of the body. Many scholars prefer the plain sense and do not insist on the fingerprint reading.

title: Fiqh
def: Islamic jurisprudence: the scholars’ work of understanding and applying the sharia.
what: Fiqh means “understanding”, and the Quran uses the idea of seeking understanding in the religion (9:122). The four main Sunni schools, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali, and other schools such as the Ja’fari and Ibadi, each reached rulings by a method of reading the sources, and they often disagree.
misread: That Islamic law is one rulebook with one answer on each question.
sources: Disagreement among the schools is normal and long recognised. A ruling is a scholar’s judgement of what the sources require, offered with its evidence, and a Muslim chooses a qualified scholar to follow. Many things people call “Islamic law” in the news are a particular government’s choice among such opinions, or custom, not the sources themselves.

title: Fire
def: The Quran uses fire as a sign of God’s provision (56:71) and as the image of Hell.
what: “Have you seen the fire that you kindle? Is it you who made its tree grow, or are We the grower? We made it a reminder and a benefit for the wayfarers” (56:71–73). The Quran also says that the Fire is fuelled with “people and stones” (2:24), and calls Hell “the Fire”.

title: Fitna
def: Trial, persecution or turmoil; in the Quran, mainly the persecution of believers for their faith.
what: The root means to test, as gold is tried in fire. The Quran says God tests people with good and evil as a trial (21:35). In the verses on fighting it means persecution: “fitna is worse than killing” (2:191, also 2:217).
misread: That “fight them until there is no fitna” (2:193) means fighting until everyone converts.
sources: The verse continues: “if they cease, there is no hostility except against the wrongdoers” (2:193). The fighting is to stop persecution, and the Muslims in Mecca had been tortured and driven out for their belief. It sits in the same chapter that says there is “no compulsion in religion” (2:256) and is read together with it.

title: Fitra
def: The innate disposition with which every person is born, inclined to recognise God.
what: “So set your face to the religion, upright; the fiṭra of God upon which He created people” (30:30). The Prophet said: “Every child is born in a state of fiṭra; then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian or a Magian” (Sahih al-Bukhari). A list of acts of fitra includes clipping nails, trimming the moustache, circumcision, and shaving the pubic hair (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: The idea is that no child is born in sin: every person starts with a natural recognition of his Creator.

title: Five pillars
def: The five basic acts of Islam: the declaration of faith, prayer, zakat, fasting in Ramadan and the pilgrimage.
what: The Prophet said: “Islam is built on five: testifying that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, establishing prayer, giving zakat, pilgrimage to the House, and fasting Ramadan” (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). Zakat is due on wealth above a minimum, and the pilgrimage only of those able.

title: Forgetting
def: The Quran says that God will make the Prophet recite so that he does not forget except what God wills (87:6–7), and some verses were caused to be forgotten.
what: “We shall make you recite, and you will not forget, except what God wills” (87:6–7). The Quran also says that whatever verse God abrogates or causes to be forgotten, He replaces by a better one (2:106). A report in Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet’s saying, on hearing a man recite, “May God have mercy on him: he reminded me of verses I had been caused to forget.”
misread: That Muhammad’s forgetting of verses shows the Quran was not preserved.
sources: Muslims hold that these cases are what the Quran itself describes: verses lifted by God’s will, as part of naskh, and a human being’s forgetting of what he had not been commanded to keep. The Quran as it is was preserved by recitation and in writing, and Muslims believe God’s promise to guard it (15:9).

title: Forgiveness
def: God forgives all sins for those who repent; the Quran also urges forgiveness between people.
what: “Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God; God forgives all sins; He is the Forgiving, the Merciful” (39:53). Only associating partners with Him is not forgiven unless repented of (4:48). The Quran says: “let them pardon and overlook; do you not love that God should forgive you?” (24:22), a verse about Abu Bakr, who had cut off support to a relative who spread slander about his daughter Aisha, and then resumed it.

title: Freedom
def: Islam teaches freedom of belief and liberation from servitude to anything but God; the Quran also retells the exodus from Egypt.
what: “Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve” (18:29). The Quran tells how Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt (20:77, 2:49–50). Muslims also say that submission to God sets a person free of submission to other human beings. A saying attributed to Caliph Umar asks: “Since when have you enslaved people, when their mothers bore them free?”

title: Friday
def: The day of congregational prayer, which the Quran says should interrupt trade for a time and then allow people to disperse for their work (62:9–10).
what: “O you who believe, when the call to prayer is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of God and leave trade. That is better for you… And when the prayer is done, disperse in the land and seek God’s bounty, and remember God often” (62:9–10). The Friday prayer has a sermon and two units. The Prophet said that Friday is the best day on which the sun rises (Sahih Muslim).
sources: Friday is not a day of rest: the Quran says to resume work after the prayer. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that God led earlier communities away from Friday, giving the Jews the Sabbath and the Christians Sunday, and guided the Muslims to it.

title: Funeral
def: The Muslim rites for the dead: washing, shrouding, a funeral prayer, and prompt burial in a simple grave.
what: The body is washed, wrapped in plain white cloth, prayed over by the community in a prayer without bowing or prostration, and buried quickly, facing the Kaaba. The Prophet said “hasten with the funeral” (Sahih al-Bukhari), and discouraged mourning beyond three days, other than for a widow (four months and ten days). The Quran’s story of the raven that showed Cain how to bury his brother (5:31) is the earliest mention of burial.

title: Furqan
def: “The criterion”: the Quran’s name for itself and for the Torah, and the day of Badr.
what: “Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to all the worlds” (25:1). “The month of Ramadan in which the Quran was sent down, a guidance for people and clear proofs of guidance and the Criterion” (2:185). God also gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion (21:48), and the day of Badr is “the Day of the Criterion” (8:41). The word means that which separates truth from falsehood, and some scholars say it is a loanword from Aramaic purqānā, “salvation”.

title: Fahishah, al-
def: A grave and shameful sin, such as adultery.
what: Al-fāḥisha and al-faḥshāʾ name an act so gross that it offends both revelation and decency. The Quran uses the word for adultery: “Do not approach adultery; it is an indecency and an evil way” (17:32). It also says that God has forbidden “shameful deeds, whether open or hidden” (7:33), which shows that the term covers private wrongs as well as public ones.

Scholars read it as a class of major sins with a fixed penalty or a strong moral censure, and adultery is the clearest case. The Quran links prayer with the restraint of such conduct: “Prayer keeps one away from indecency and what is wrong” (29:45). The plural fawāḥish is used for these deeds in general. The word therefore serves as a standing warning against the gravest moral failings.
misread: Translated as “immorality” or “lewdness”, which can suggest a matter of taste; the Arabic names an act of grave sin that God has forbidden.

title: Fakkara
def: To think and ponder, and in the end to perceive and know the patterns and will of God.
what: Fakkara means to reflect with effort, turning a matter over until its meaning is clear. In the Quran this reflection has a direction: it moves from the signs of creation to their Maker. After naming rain, crops, night and day, sun and moon, the Quran says: “In that are signs for people who reflect” (16:11–12). Believers are described as those who “reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth” (3:191). The verb is one of the Quran’s favored ways to invite the reader to think.

The same word underlies tafakkur, the practice of contemplating the world as evidence of God’s power and care. Faruqi treats it as the thinking that ends in knowledge of the divine patterns and will, so that thought is an act of worship as well as an exercise of the mind. For this reason, the Muslim tradition has never treated serious thought as opposed to faith.
misread: Thought is sometimes taken to be a secular activity apart from faith; the Quran presents reflection on creation as a path to knowing God.

title: Falah
def: Success in reaching full conviction and realization of the divine will; the lasting success promised to those who obey God.
what: Falāḥ is the success that endures, and the Quran reserves it for those who live by God’s guidance. Surah 23 opens: “Successful indeed are the believers” (23:1), and describes them by their humble prayer, their trustworthiness and their care for charity. Another verse says: “He who purifies himself has succeeded” (87:14). The Quran uses the verb form aflaḥa, “has succeeded”, for such people.

The word is heard five times a day in the call to prayer, in the phrase ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ, “come to success”. Placed beside “come to prayer”, it tells the listener where real success lies. Faruqi defines it as full conviction and realization of God’s will, which is a larger idea than prosperity or winning. Its opposite is khusrān, loss. Success in this sense is measured by the verdict of God and not by the world.
misread: Usually translated “prosperity” or “success”, which suggests worldly gain; the Quranic term means success before God, in this life and the next.

title: Faqaha
def: To understand the ordinances of God, His revelation and His patterns in creation, which makes it a synonym of ʿilm; also to know Islamic law and apply it properly.
what: Faqaha means to grasp a matter with understanding, and it is the verb from which fiqh comes. The Quran calls on a party from every group to go out “to gain deep understanding in religion” and to warn their people on return (9:122). It also speaks of those who have hearts with which they “do not understand” (7:179), and the word there is the same root.

In its wide sense the verb is close to ʿilm, knowledge of what God has revealed and of how He has ordered creation. In its narrower sense it names knowledge of the rules of Islamic law and the skill to apply them. The Prophet said: “If God wants good for a person, He gives him understanding in religion” (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).
misread: Reduced to “jurisprudence”, which drops the first and wider sense of understanding God’s revelation and His order in creation.

title: Faqih
def: A person of deep understanding of religion, used for a jurist and as a synonym of ʿālim; the plural is fuqahāʾ.
what: A faqīh is one who has fiqh, a thorough understanding of the religion. The plural is fuqahāʾ. In the sense Faruqi gives, it is a synonym of ʿālim, a person of knowledge. In common use it names a jurist who can draw out legal rulings from the Quran and the sunna and give an answer to a question of practice.

The Quran’s call for people to gain understanding in religion and to teach it (9:122) is the basis for the standing of such scholars. The great jurists, among them Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafiʿi and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, are called fuqahāʾ. The title does not require a state office; it rests on learning and character, and the community looks to the faqīh for guidance.
misread: Rendered “jurist” alone, which omits the older sense in which the faqīh is simply a scholar who understands the religion.

title: Fasaqa
def: To commit sin, or to follow a course of sinfulness and evil that stops short of apostasy or blasphemy.
what: Fasaqa means to depart from obedience to God by sinning, while remaining within the faith. The one who does so is a fāsiq, and the state is fisq or fusūq. The Quran lists three things that God has made hateful to the believer: disbelief, fusūq and disobedience (49:7). The word thus marks a lesser rank than disbelief but a serious one.

Jurists apply the title fāsiq to a Muslim who persists in major sins or openly disregards the law. The Quran tells believers: “If a fāsiq brings you news, verify it” (49:6), and the jurists take from this that the testimony of such a person is to be examined with care. The term does not strip a person of Islam. The term thus marks a grave failing within the community of the faithful.
misread: Translated “wickedness” or “evil”, which can read as unbelief; the term names sinful conduct that falls short of apostasy or blasphemy.

title: Fataha
def: Said of God: to grant His servants victory over their enemies, or to open a way out of their difficulties, moral or material.
what: Fataha means to open. When God is the subject, it means He opens a path for His servants, whether by giving them victory over an enemy or by releasing them from a hardship. “Whatever mercy God opens for people, none can withhold it” (35:2). Surah 48 begins: “Truly We have granted you a clear victory” (48:1), using the same root.

The Quran also uses the verb for blessings opened to those of faith: “Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from heaven and earth” (7:96). In this sense the verb joins the moral and the material. A breakthrough in the heart, such as guidance or relief from despair, is as much a gift of God as success in battle.
misread: Rendered “to conquer”, which narrows an act of divine opening that may be moral as well as military.

title: Fatana
def: To beguile, mislead or draw someone away from the straight path, al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm.
what: Fatana means to put to trial, and by extension to lure a person off course. The Quran uses it of efforts to turn the Prophet from his message: “They were about to tempt you away from what We revealed to you” (17:73). Another verse warns him to “beware lest they tempt you away from part of what God has sent down to you” (5:49). In each case the verb describes an attempt to separate a person from what God has revealed.

The same root gives fitna, a trial or a cause of temptation, and maftūn, one who has been led astray. Faruqi’s gloss stresses the direction: the person is drawn away from al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm, the path of guidance that Muslims ask for in every rakʿa of prayer. The verb can describe the work of a human tempter or of Satan. It is therefore a word of warning for every believer.
misread: Often rendered “to tempt” alone, which does not show that the temptation leads away from the straight path.

title: Fath
def: The act of opening or granting, as in fataha, and the victory or breakthrough that is granted; the plural is al-futūḥāt.
what: Fatḥ is the noun of fataha: the opening that God grants and the victory or breakthrough that results. Surah 48 is called al-Fatḥ, and its first verse reads: “We have granted you a clear victory” (48:1). Surah 110 opens: “When the help of God and the victory (al-fatḥ) come” (110:1). The word is thus linked to the greatest events of the Prophet’s life.

Muslim writers have often used fatḥ for the peaceful entry of the Prophet into Mecca in the eighth year after the hijra, where the term implies the opening of a city and of hearts to the faith. Its plural, al-futūḥāt, names the successive victories of the early community. Faruqi asks that the Arabic term be kept, because “conquest” shows only the material side. It also conveys that the result belongs to God, who grants it.
misread: Translated “conquest”, which reads as military seizure; the Arabic term stresses an opening granted by God.

title: Fatih, al-
def: Divine names meaning He Who grants fatḥ, and He Who always grants it: the Opener, the One Who opens the way to victory and relief.
what: Al-Fattāḥ is among the traditional ninety-nine names of God, and it occurs in the Quran: “He is the All-Knowing Fattāḥ” (34:26), a phrase usually rendered “the All-Knowing Judge”, because the word also means one who decides a matter. Al-Fātiḥ is the plain agent form, God as the one who opens. Both forms are drawn from fataha, which means to open.

The intensive fattāḥ says that God opens again and again. He opens the way to victory, as in 48:1, and the doors of mercy and provision (35:2). Believers invoke the name when they ask for relief from a hardship, and for the opening of understanding. Faruqi’s gloss ties both names to fatḥ, the breakthrough that God alone grants. The believer may therefore ask Him to open a door that seems closed.
misread: Rendered “the Judge” or “the Opener” as though one meaning exhausted it; the Quranic usage joins opening a way with deciding a matter.

title: Fatihah, al-
def: The opening surah of the Noble Quran.
what: Al-Fātiḥa is the first surah of the Quran, of seven verses. Its name means “the Opening”. It begins with praise of God, Lord of the worlds, and states the pledge “You alone we worship, and from You alone we seek help” (1:5). It closes with the prayer to be guided on the straight path (1:6–7). The Quran refers to “the seven oft-repeated verses” (15:87), which commentators relate to it.

Muslims recite al-Fātiḥa in every rakʿa of the prayer. The Prophet said that there is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). It is also recited at many other moments, including the opening of gatherings, and over the sick in supplication. It holds in brief the aims of the whole Quran.
misread: Sometimes called “the Lord’s Prayer of Islam”, which borrows a Christian category; the Muslim term is the Opening of the Book, recited within each prayer.

title: Fawatih al-Suwar
def: The letters of the Arabic alphabet that stand at the head of a number of surahs.
what: Twenty-nine surahs of the Quran open with one or more letters of the Arabic alphabet, read out by their names and not as words. The first is surah 2, which begins Alif Lām Mīm (2:1). Others include Yā Sīn (36:1), Qāf (50:1) and Nūn (68:1). In all, fourteen different letters are used, alone or in combination. The Quran’s reciters pronounce them letter by letter.

Their meaning is not settled. Some commentators say they are among the matters that God alone knows. Others propose that they point to the fact that the Quran is built of the very letters the Arabs used, and yet cannot be matched (compare 2:23). Many of these surahs go on at once to speak of the Book’s revelation. The term is also given as al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa, the disjoined letters.
misread: Called “mysterious letters” as if a hidden code; scholars treat them as an opening feature of the revelation whose sense is disputed or known to God.

title: Fikr
def: Thought and intellection in their general sense.
what: Fikr is the general word for thought: the act of the mind in considering a matter, together with its product. It is the noun related to the verb fakkara, to ponder. Where fakkara in the Quran leads to the signs of God in creation, fikr is used in later Arabic writing for thought of every kind, including philosophy and the thinking of a school or a movement.

Muslim authors have produced a long literature on fikr. The phrase al-fikr al-islāmī, Islamic thought, refers to the body of thinking developed by scholars in theology, law, ethics and the sciences. In the Quran the related verbal forms are always positive, and the book urges people to reflect (6:50, 16:44). The noun itself is not found in the Quran, which uses verb forms.
misread: Treated as a neutral word for any thinking; in Muslim usage it is tied to the call to reflect on God’s signs.

title: Futuhat, al-
def: The moral and material victories granted to Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his early followers, and so the conversion of whole populations to Islam.
what: Al-futūḥāt is the plural of fatḥ, an opening or victory granted by God. It names the series of victories that came to Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the early community, beginning with the opening of Mecca and extending to Syria, Iraq, Egypt, Persia and further. The word covers both the military outcome and the spread of the faith. The unit of meaning is thus the victory as God’s gift, whatever its field.

Faruqi’s definition goes further than the common sense of “the conquests”. He includes the moral victories, and the entry of whole populations into Islam, as part of what the term means. The Quran gives the pattern: “When the help of God and the victory come, and you see people entering the religion of God in crowds” (110:1–2). The book of Ibn ʿArabī called al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya uses the same word for another kind of opening, the spiritual. The meaning is therefore wider than the English word “conquests” allows.
misread: Rendered “the Islamic conquests”, which reduces the term to military expansion; it also covers the moral victories and the entry of peoples into Islam.
